title: Why Madeira tastes the way it does

lede.text: Terraced slopes of mostly basaltic soil with a low pH give Madeira its high acidity. That acidity is behind the wine's well-known long life.

chapters.title: Islands in the open Atlantic
paras: Madeira lies in the Atlantic Ocean between 30° and 33° north, 978 km southwest of Lisbon. It is about 700 km from the African coast, at almost the same latitude as Casablanca.
Two inhabited islands make up the wine region: Madeira itself at 740.7 km² and Porto Santo at 42.5 km². The grapes must come from these islands only.

fly.caption: The larger of the two inhabited islands, 740.7 km² in the Atlantic.

chapters.title: A mild year with little swing
paras: Temperatures vary little through the growing cycle. During ripening they are normally mild.
Altitude and exposure shape microclimates from plot to plot, and these strongly mark the grapes.

chapters.title: Hand-built terraces on volcanic soil
paras: The soils are mostly of basaltic origin, with a low pH. They give musts and wines their high acidity.
The slopes are steep, so growers built poios, terraces that make farming possible. Farmland is scarce, so organic matter is often added to the soil and its levels are usually high.
Plots are small and the land is rugged. Machines are almost never an option, so most work in the vineyard is done by hand, from harvest to pruning.
Vines are trained in three ways. The most common are the latada (a pergola), the espaldeira (a trellis) and vines grown low on the ground.

chapters.title: Fortified, then aged
paras: Madeira is a fortified wine (vinho licoroso). Fortifying and ageing are its two keystones. Neutral wine alcohol of at least 96% vol is added during or after fermentation. No still white, rosado or sparkling wine is part of the rules.
Dozens of grapes are listed, both white and red. Four are named on labels, each with a sweetness: Sercial is dry, Verdelho medium-dry, Boal medium-sweet and Malvasia sweet.

Two methods exist. With canteiro, the wine ages in wood for at least 2 consecutive years and is sold 36 months after the last fortification. With estufagem, the fortified wine is held in containers at no more than 50 °C for at least 90 days.
Yields are capped at 80 hl of must per hectare.
The wines are fresh, thanks to their typical acidity. Dry types are light and balanced. Sweeter ones are fuller, with caramel, and all share dried fruit and wood notes and a long finish.
Garrafeira (or Frasqueira) is wine of exceptional quality, aged in wood from a single harvest. Colheita is good-quality wine from one harvest, with dried fruit, caramel and honey notes.

terms.text: A dry or medium-dry, fine and light wine with good acidity, with notes of orange peel and vanilla.
A grape name on the label for a wine that can be dry, medium-dry, medium-sweet or sweet.
Wines may state 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 or more than 40 years, and the bouquet grows more intense with age.
